strengths: The paper addresses five highly relevant, underrepresented languages and links a potentially valuable collection of compact pretrained and instruction-tuned models, language-specific tokenizers, and instruction data.

Training 108M–367M parameter models on a single A100 is a practically meaningful contribution. The paper reports architecture, optimizer, approximate training time, token counts, inference speed, and compute utilization.

The empirical scope is broad: several reasoning and comprehension benchmarks, many multilingual baselines, tokenizer/data/context ablations across languages, perplexity measurements, and an attempted human evaluation.
The 5K native-authored Bangla instruction set and attention to morphology, corpus cleaning, and language-specific modeling are worthwhile resource-building efforts.
weaknesses: The proposed RoPE method does not substantiate its central efficiency claim. Compressing position indices cannot reduce attention's quadratic memory or computation, so it cannot make a sequence that exceeds hardware memory fit. Positional interpolation is also established prior work. The ablation jointly changes sequence length, training-token count, and compute, lacks an ordinary-RoPE control at the same length, and includes no long-context evaluation.

Much of the reported base-model performance is approximately chance: about 25.22 versus roughly 25 for Bangla, 30.97 versus roughly 30.6 for Hindi, and similarly small margins for Marathi, Tamil, and Telugu. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or training-seed variation are provided, yet differences of tenths of a point are treated as meaningful wins. Averaging accuracies across tasks with different chance levels further obscures the evidence.

The headline comparisons are not controlled for pretraining data, token budget, instruction tuning, prompting format, or model type. In particular, instruction-tuned Paramanu models are frequently compared with base models, and the multilingual model is not a matched monolingual-versus-multilingual control. These results cannot establish that monolingual modeling is an optimal strategy or demonstrate a curse of multilinguality.

The morphology claim is insufficiently validated. Vocabulary sizes, fertility definition and evaluation corpus are omitted; only a few selected segmentations are linguistically inspected; and the description of a Viterbi search combining deterministic BPE merges with Unigram scores is algorithmically unclear. The BPE ablation does not establish equal parameter counts, vocabulary capacity, raw-text exposure, or compute, and it has no replicated runs or morphological gold evaluation.

Reproducibility is undermined by substantial omissions and contradictions. Examples include Telugu XStoryCloze scores of 51.42 versus 54.20 for apparently the same full model, Marathi ARC scores of 26.49 versus 26.94, training-token totals that do not follow from the stated steps, batch sizes, accumulation, and sequence lengths, and conflicting 23K versus 27K instruction counts. The additional 52K Hindi Alpaca examples appear only in the results discussion. Exact tokenizer configurations, evaluation prompts/chat templates, harness versions, seeds, checkpoint selection, and training corpora for Sanskrit and mParamanu are also missing.

Several additional claims overreach the evidence. Unseen-language Devanagari results are essentially at random baselines and do not demonstrate useful cross-lingual transfer, while translation and retrieval are never evaluated. Perplexities from different tokenizers or languages are not directly comparable. The human study uses only ten prompts and selected 'top-3' generations without explaining selection, blinding, randomization, uncertainty, or per-dimension results; it also inconsistently mentions Sanskrit despite saying only Bangla and Hindi were evaluated. Overall, extensive new controls, corrected reporting, and a more rigorous evaluation are needed before the contribution is sound and reproducible enough for Findings.

The proposed mapping p′=pL/y is essentially standard positional interpolation from Chen et al. (2023), and scaling position indices does not reduce the quadratic attention memory required by a longer token sequence. Table 5 changes context length and interpolation factor together, lacks an unscaled same-length control and long-context evaluation, and therefore cannot show either memory efficiency or an interpolation benefit. Its claimed monotonic improvement is also contradicted by the reported Bangla, Hindi, and Tamil numbers.","The headline model comparisons are not rigorous enough to establish that Paramanu outperforms larger models. Many scores are at or only slightly above chance; differences are often below two points, yet there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated runs, or benchmark sample sizes. Prompt formats, likelihood normalization, chat templates, model revisions, and detailed evaluation settings are omitted, while base and instruction-tuned baselines are mixed.","Several central results are internally inconsistent. Telugu XStoryCloze is 51.42 in Table 13, 54.20 in Tables 4–5, and 56.06 in Table 14; the corresponding averages differ. The Marathi “full” results differ between Tables 4 and 5, and the stated Hindi tokenizer gain does not match Table 4 arithmetic. Instruction-data counts alternate between 23K and 27K, and the main text suggests post-editing for all translated languages whereas the appendix says only Hindi and Marathi were post-edited.","The claim of morphological alignment is based mainly on selected word examples. There is no gold morphological-boundary evaluation, linguistic annotation study, or analysis by phenomenon. Vocabulary sizes are not reported, and the tokenizer ablation does not establish that vocabulary size, embedding parameter count, training-token count, and other conditions are controlled; consequently, neither the causal morphology claim nor the asserted cost reduction is demonstrated.","The cross-lingual-transfer interpretation is unsound. The Marathi and Sanskrit models’ Hindi task scores are approximately the chance baselines for the constituent 2-, 3-, and 4-way tasks, so averaging them to about 31 does not demonstrate strong transfer. The argument based on perplexity is also invalid because perplexities obtained with different tokenizers and apparently different language validation sets are not directly comparable. No translation or retrieval experiment supports the downstream-transfer claims.","Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the artifact release. The manuscript omits vocabulary construction parameters, exact corpus versions and unique-token/epoch counts, cleaning rules, random seeds, data packing, μP details, training code, evaluation configurations, and most instruction-tuning settings. The annotation-dataset Fleiss-kappa calculation is likewise uninterpretable without shared-item and label details.","These concerns affect soundness rather than merely novelty or excitement. The released resources are promising, but the central methodological and comparative conclusions require reconciliation, substantial reanalysis, controlled experiments, and narrower claims before the work meets the Findings threshold. A revised submission could plausibly be prepared for a future cycle."]}

The empirical scope is ambitious: five languages, models of 108M–367M parameters, numerous multilingual baselines up to 8B, multiple downstream tasks, tokenizer/data ablations, efficiency measurements, and an attempted human evaluation.
The hybrid BPE–Unigram approach is plausibly motivated, and Table 4 reports gains over BPE across all five languages. The focus on language-specific preprocessing and tokenization is worthwhile.

The paper reports useful implementation information, including model dimensions, optimizer settings, processed-token counts, GPU hours, inference speed, and major corpus sources, while openly acknowledging data limitations, repeated epochs, translation artifacts, and incomplete convergence.
weaknesses: The RoPE contribution is not technically supported. The proposed mapping p′=pL/y is essentially standard positional interpolation from Chen et al. (2023), and scaling position indices does not reduce the quadratic attention memory required by a longer token sequence. Table 5 changes context length and interpolation factor together, lacks an unscaled same-length control and long-context evaluation, and therefore cannot show either memory efficiency or an interpolation benefit. Its claimed monotonic improvement is also contradicted by the reported Bangla, Hindi, and Tamil numbers.

The headline model comparisons are not rigorous enough to establish that Paramanu outperforms larger models. Many scores are at or only slightly above chance; differences are often below two points, yet there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated runs, or benchmark sample sizes. Prompt formats, likelihood normalization, chat templates, model revisions, and detailed evaluation settings are omitted, while base and instruction-tuned baselines are mixed.

Several central results are internally inconsistent. Telugu XStoryCloze is 51.42 in Table 13, 54.20 in Tables 4–5, and 56.06 in Table 14; the corresponding averages differ. The Marathi “full” results differ between Tables 4 and 5, and the stated Hindi tokenizer gain does not match Table 4 arithmetic. Instruction-data counts alternate between 23K and 27K, and the main text suggests post-editing for all translated languages whereas the appendix says only Hindi and Marathi were post-edited.

The claim of morphological alignment is based mainly on selected word examples. There is no gold morphological-boundary evaluation, linguistic annotation study, or analysis by phenomenon. Vocabulary sizes are not reported, and the tokenizer ablation does not establish that vocabulary size, embedding parameter count, training-token count, and other conditions are controlled; consequently, neither the causal morphology claim nor the asserted cost reduction is demonstrated.

The cross-lingual-transfer interpretation is unsound. The Marathi and Sanskrit models’ Hindi task scores are approximately the chance baselines for the constituent 2-, 3-, and 4-way tasks, so averaging them to about 31 does not demonstrate strong transfer. The argument based on perplexity is also invalid because perplexities obtained with different tokenizers and apparently different language validation sets are not directly comparable. No translation or retrieval experiment supports the downstream-transfer claims.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the artifact release. The manuscript omits vocabulary construction parameters, exact corpus versions and unique-token/epoch counts, cleaning rules, random seeds, data packing, μP details, training code, evaluation configurations, and most instruction-tuning settings. The sub-$1,000 claim lacks a stated provider/rate and apparently excludes annotation and translation costs.

The human evaluation is too under-specified to validate generation quality: “top-3 responses” suggests an unexplained selection step; prompt selection, decoding, annotator assignment, blinding, compensation, and rating aggregation are missing; no uncertainty is reported; and Sanskrit agreement is given despite the study being described as Bangla/Hindi evaluation. The annotation-dataset Fleiss-kappa calculation is likewise uninterpretable without shared-item and label details.

These concerns affect soundness rather than merely novelty or excitement. The released resources are promising, but the central methodological and comparative conclusions require reconciliation, substantial reanalysis, controlled experiments, and narrower claims before the work meets the Findings threshold. A revised submission could plausibly be prepared for a future cycle.

strengths: Addresses an important, highly relevant NLP problem: affordable language modeling for five widely spoken, morphologically rich Indian languages. The compact model family and single-GPU focus could materially benefit under-resourced research communities. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-q90jl4le/call-f2f7580022d64ea3aadcf8931a3b4586/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The work offers a potentially valuable resource bundle—monolingual pretrained and instruction-tuned models, language-specific tokenizers, and instruction data—and points to publicly available artifacts.

The experimental scope is ambitious: five languages, numerous multilingual baselines up to 8B parameters, component ablations, perplexity, efficiency measurements, and some human evaluation. Reporting GPU hours and acknowledging repeated-data training are useful transparency steps.

The 5,000 human-authored Bangla instruction-response pairs produced by 20 native speakers could be a meaningful dataset contribution, and the paper candidly acknowledges domain limitations, machine-translation artifacts, incomplete convergence, and safety risks.
weaknesses: The central competitiveness claim is not adequately supported because most base-model results are essentially at chance: Bangla averages 25.22 versus a 25% baseline; Hindi 30.97 versus approximately 30.56 for its mixture of four-way, binary, and three-way tasks; Marathi 26.40 versus 25; Tamil 33.34 versus 31.25; and Telugu 32.22 versus 31.25. Numerically exceeding baselines that themselves score at or below chance does not demonstrate useful language understanding. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-seed results establish that the small differences are meaningful, while the strongest comparisons often place instruction-tuned Paramanu models against untuned baselines.

The claimed RoPE contribution is substantially the positional-interpolation method already introduced by Chen et al. (2023), using the same linear rescaling. More seriously, scaling position indices does not reduce the memory or quadratic attention cost of processing y tokens and therefore cannot by itself make a hardware-infeasible sequence fit. Table 5 jointly changes actual sequence length and the scaling factor, lacks a standard-RoPE control at the same sequence length and compute budget, and includes no genuinely long-context evaluation. Thus neither novelty nor the claimed training-efficiency mechanism is established.

The tokenizer evidence does not establish morphological alignment. Fertility is not a morphology metric, the cross-model fertility numbers come from another source without a specified common evaluation corpus, and only selected segmentation examples are presented. Adding all Unigram pieces changes vocabulary size, embedding parameters, and raw-text coverage per fixed token budget, but vocabulary sizes and parameter-matched controls are absent. There is also no pure-Unigram baseline, expert boundary annotation, seed variance, or statistical analysis.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate. The paper omits exact vocabulary sizes, data manifests and licenses, split construction, preprocessing rules/code, contamination checks, random seeds, evaluation prompts and scoring/normalization settings, generation parameters, CPU specifications, and training/evaluation code. Several accounts conflict: 23K versus 27K Bangla instructions; an otherwise unexplained 52K Alpaca component for Hindi; inconsistent post-editing scope; and token totals that do not follow from the steps, batch sizes, accumulation, sequence lengths, and model configurations reported in Tables 3 and 16. Identical or apparently identical configurations also receive different scores across Tables 4, 5, and 13.

Evaluation validity needs substantial strengthening. There is no benchmark decontamination despite web and Wikipedia pretraining, no sample counts or uncertainty, and raw accuracies with different chance levels are averaged together. Perplexities across different tokenizers/languages are not directly comparable, and the cost/latency claim lacks matched inference baselines and a documented cost calculation.

The cross-lingual-transfer and human-evaluation conclusions are overdrawn. Sanskrit and multilingual models evaluated on Hindi/Marathi remain approximately at chance, yet this is interpreted as strong transfer and extrapolated to translation and retrieval without testing either task. Human evaluation uses only ten prompts and unspecified “top-3” responses, with no selection, decoding, blinding, randomization, annotator-demographic, compensation, or uncertainty details; it covers only a subset of languages, and the referenced agreement figure is missing (“Figure ??”).

The resource direction is promising, but these are decisive soundness and reproducibility problems rather than merely reservations about novelty or excitement. Substantial re-analysis, controlled experiments, consistency corrections, and fuller artifact documentation are needed before the work meets the Findings threshold.

strengths: The work targets five widely spoken, under-resourced Indian languages and releases tangible artifacts: compact pretrained and instruction-tuned models, tokenizers, and instruction data. This is highly relevant to inclusive NLP research.

The emphasis on sub-400M models trained on one A100 is practically valuable. The paper reports parameter counts, training hours, token totals, throughput, perplexity, and hardware utilization, offering more efficiency information than many model papers.

The evaluation is broad in language and baseline coverage, and the instruction-tuned checkpoints show potentially meaningful gains—particularly Hindi, whose reported average rises from 30.97 to 40.14.

The motivation for language-specific tokenization is sensible, and the authors appropriately acknowledge limited domain coverage, repeated data, machine-translation artifacts, incomplete convergence, and safety limitations.
weaknesses: The headline superiority claim is not adequately established. Most pretrained results are essentially at chance: Bangla averages 25.22 on four-choice tasks; Hindi averages 30.97 against a mixed-task chance average of about 30.6; and Telugu averages 32.22 against about 31.25. Many claimed wins over larger models are only 1–2 points, with no sample counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated seeds. Counting how many larger models are beaten therefore largely ranks chance-level fluctuations. Comparisons also mix base and instruction-tuned checkpoints without consistently identifying exact variants.

The RoPE contribution is neither convincingly novel nor technically supported. Its formula is the positional-interpolation method already cited from Chen et al. Scaling position indices does not reduce the sequence-length-dependent memory or quadratic attention computation, so it cannot itself make a longer sequence fit constrained hardware. Table 5 simultaneously changes interpolation factor and context length—and apparently tokens/FLOPs—without standard-RoPE, fixed-token, or fixed-compute controls. No long-context task or position-stratified perplexity evaluation demonstrates learned long-range dependencies.

The tokenizer description appears internally inconsistent: a SentencePiece model has one encoding model type, whereas the paper simultaneously claims deterministic BPE merges and Unigram-style Viterbi search over their union. The implementation is not released or specified sufficiently to resolve this. Adding every missing Unigram piece may also increase vocabulary size, embedding parameters, and effective capacity, but vocabulary sizes and parameter-matched controls are absent. Hand-selected examples and fertility alone do not establish morphological alignment, and no gold morphological-boundary evaluation is provided.

There are numerous material reporting contradictions. The stated 54.6 GB corpus disagrees with the 56.1 GB sum in Table 1. Listed token totals conflict with the stated batch sizes, accumulation, sequence lengths, and claim that all models except Hindi ran for 100K steps. Instruction data are variously described as 23K or 27K, with an additional 52K Hindi Alpaca set mentioned only in the appendix; the main text claims post-editing for all translated languages whereas the appendix says only Hindi and Marathi. Telugu XStoryCloze is reported as 51.42, 54.20, and 56.06 in different tables. These inconsistencies prevent tracing results to checkpoints and configurations.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the artifact release. There is no training/evaluation code link, and essential details are missing: vocabulary construction settings and sizes, cleaning and language-ID thresholds, unique-token/epoch counts, random seeds, checkpoint-selection rules, benchmark versions and sample sizes, translation-quality checks, prompt templates, LM-Eval revision/options, and decoding or likelihood-scoring configurations. Benchmark decontamination is also not addressed.

Several broader conclusions are overclaimed. The cross-lingual Devanagari results are near chance, and perplexities from different corpora/tokenizers are not directly comparable evidence of transfer; translation and retrieval are not evaluated despite claims about those applications. The Sanskrit and multilingual models are introduced late without adequate training-data documentation. Human evaluation uses only ten prompts and leaves response selection (“top-3”), generation settings, blinding, randomization, per-criterion results, and uncertainty unclear; its Sanskrit/kappa statements and unresolved “Figure ??” reference are also inconsistent. Substantial controlled reevaluation and documentation are needed before the work meets Findings-level soundness, although the existing resources make a next-cycle resubmission plausible.

strengths: The manuscript tackles an important ACL-relevant problem: affordable language modeling for five under-served Indian languages spanning four scripts and two language families. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-e6gc74uy/call-fe422571f62449e3a3497e776f6a4303/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The linked release of compact models, tokenizers, and instruction data could become a useful community resource. Reporting single-GPU hours and processed-token counts also foregrounds accessibility.
The empirical scope is ambitious: numerous multilingual baselines, five languages, tokenizer/data-cleaning ablations, perplexity and efficiency measurements, and human evaluation.

The 5,000 native-authored Bangla instruction-response pairs, cultural-domain guidelines, and explicit discussion of data limitations, repeated epochs, translation noise, and safety risks are valuable elements.
weaknesses: The main competitiveness claim is not supported robustly. Base-model averages are only approximately 0.2 points above chance for Bangla, 0.4 for Hindi, 1.4 for Marathi, 2.1 for Tamil, and 1.0 for Telugu. Many compared systems are also at or below chance, so ranking above them does not demonstrate useful capability. The claimed Hindi/Marathi cross-lingual transfer is especially weak: reported averages are essentially chance. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated seeds accompany the small differences.

Evaluation is insufficiently specified for reproduction: the manuscript omits prompt templates, harness version/commit, choice-scoring and normalization details, exact splits and sample counts, checkpoint selection, and contamination checks. Comparing heterogeneous base and instruction-tuned systems further complicates interpretation. The human study lacks generation settings, blinding/randomization details, uncertainty, and a clear explanation of “top-3 responses”; the appendix even contains an unresolved Figure ?? reference.

The RoPE contribution is conceptually and empirically unconvincing. Linear rescaling of positions is established positional interpolation, and rescaling position indices does not reduce the memory needed to process a longer sequence. Table 5 perfectly confounds context length with the scaling factor, lacks an unscaled same-length control and any long-context task, and therefore cannot attribute gains to interpolation. Its claimed monotonic trend is also contradicted by decreases shown for Bangla, Hindi, and Tamil.

The hybrid tokenizer is not reproducible or adequately validated. The stated Viterbi competition is inconsistent with standard SentencePiece BPE behavior unless the final model type and algorithm are changed, yet neither model type nor score calibration is given. Vocabulary sizes are omitted, making fertility and model-capacity comparisons uncontrolled. A few selected segmentations and fertility against unrelated tokenizers do not establish morphological alignment; a controlled same-vocabulary baseline and gold morphological-boundary evaluation are needed.

Numerous internal inconsistencies undermine reproducibility. Table 1 sums to 56.1 GB rather than the stated 54.6 GB, and Hindi exceeds the claimed sub-15-GB corpus limit. Batch size × accumulation × sequence length × steps implies 26.2B tokens for Tamil/Telugu rather than 39.32B, and 78.6B for Hindi rather than 66B. Telugu results vary across tables (including 32.22 versus 32.95 averages and multiple XStoryCloze values). “Test” perplexity is reported despite only a train/validation split, and post-editing is claimed for all translations in one section but only Hindi and Marathi in another.

The tokenizer and cleaning ablations use one run and do not document matched vocabulary sizes, parameter counts, data quantities, or training tokens. The efficiency claim is likewise based mostly on parameter counts rather than controlled quality-compute or quality-latency comparisons; CPU hardware and decoding settings are missing.

Several conclusions exceed the experiments: no translation or information-retrieval task supports the asserted suitability for those applications, no long-range evaluation supports preserved dependencies, and no formal analysis establishes the claimed optimality of monolingual training. Substantial but feasible next-cycle work—protocol correction, consistency fixes, statistical evaluation, controlled ablations, and reframing or removing unsupported claims—is required before the paper meets Findings-level soundness and reproducibility.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, underserved setting and releases compact models, tokenizers, and instruction data for five major Indian languages. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-sr9zy7z6/call-368334d4730c4a889e18ff0ec3be6315/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Training language-specific 108M–367M models on one A100 is a potentially valuable demonstration of resource-conscious development, with useful reporting of model sizes, training times, throughput, and perplexity.
The evaluation spans five languages, four scripts, numerous comparison models, base and instruction-tuned variants, and several attempted ablations.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges narrow training domains, repeated data, possible non-convergence, machine-translation artifacts, and absent safety alignment.
weaknesses: The headline competitiveness claim is not adequately supported. Most base-model results are essentially at chance: approximately 25% on four-choice tasks, 50% on XStoryCloze/XCOPA, and 33% on XNLI. Averaging these heterogeneous raw accuracies obscures this fact, while tiny ranking differences are interpreted as meaningful without confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated runs.

The proposed RoPE method does not provide the claimed memory benefit: rescaling position indices changes positional phases but does not reduce the sequence length or attention-memory cost. Table 5 also changes context length and interpolation factor simultaneously, lacks an unscaled same-length baseline and long-context evaluation, and even contradicts the claimed monotonic improvement for Bangla, Hindi, and Tamil. The method closely resembles existing positional interpolation, so its novelty is also unclear.

The hybrid tokenizer is insufficiently and inconsistently specified. A SentencePiece model cannot simultaneously retain deterministic BPE merging and Unigram Viterbi behavior in the manner described without a precise new decoding algorithm. Vocabulary sizes, score calibration, and implementation details are absent. Morphological alignment is inferred from selected examples rather than gold segmentation metrics or expert evaluation, and the ablation may confound tokenizer choice with vocabulary size, raw-text exposure, and parameter count.

Several reported quantities conflict across the paper. Bangla instruction data is described as 23K and 27K examples; the Hindi setup additionally introduces 52K Alpaca examples without a consistent account; all translations are initially said to be manually post-edited, whereas the appendix says only Hindi and Marathi were. Telugu and n-shot scores differ substantially across Tables 4, 13, and 14. Token totals in Table 3 also do not reconcile with the batch sizes, accumulation factors, sequence lengths, and step counts in Table 16.

The cross-lingual-transfer conclusions are unsupported: the Hindi scores of Marathi, Sanskrit, and multilingual models are near the appropriate composite chance baseline, and perplexities measured with different tokenizers on different language corpora are not comparable. No translation or information-retrieval experiment supports the assertion that these models are well suited to those tasks.

Evaluation reproducibility and fairness are inadequate. The paper omits prompts, exact dataset configurations and sample counts, checkpoint-selection procedures, random seeds, evaluation commands, and uncertainty. Base and instruction-tuned systems are mixed in headline rankings, no contamination analysis is provided despite web/Wikipedia training data, and the statement about limited HellaSwag support due to tool issues is too vague.

The human evaluation uses only ten prompts and leaves response/model selection, blinding, randomization, annotator qualifications, rubric details, and statistical uncertainty unclear. The reported Fleiss kappa for Sanskrit conflicts with the stated Bangla/Hindi scope, and the appendix contains an unresolved figure reference. ChatGPT screenshots are largely irrelevant evidence for Paramanu.

Although artifacts are linked, the manuscript does not identify reproducible training and evaluation code or exact data manifests; preprocessing filters, the toxicity model, tokenizer construction, and cost accounting remain underspecified, while training logs are explicitly omitted. The non-commercial license also warrants qualification of the repeated claims of fully open-source and broadly usable resources. These central soundness issues require substantial new analysis and corrected experiments before Findings-level consideration.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP need: affordable, language-specific models for five widely spoken but under-resourced Indian languages. The small model sizes and single-GPU training target could make the released resources practically useful.
The experimental scope is broad, covering multiple scripts, downstream benchmarks, efficiency measurements, instruction tuning, and comparisons with models up to 8B parameters.
The authors attempt component-level evaluation of tokenization, cleaning, and context length across several languages, and report model configurations, training hours, token counts, and limitations.
The 5K human-authored Bengali instruction-response pairs, annotation guidelines, and public model/tokenizer collection are potentially valuable community resources.
weaknesses: The central RoPE claim is technically unsound as presented. Scaling positions by L/y is established positional interpolation, not a clearly new method, and it does not reduce the attention memory or computation required to process y tokens. Consequently, it cannot by itself make a sequence longer than the hardware-supported length fit in memory. Table 5 lacks a standard-RoPE baseline at the same sequence length and any long-context evaluation; its rows also appear confounded by different numbers of tokens and compute. The stated monotonic improvement is contradicted by the Bangla, Hindi, and Tamil results.

The morphology claim is inadequately validated. Unioning BPE and Unigram vocabularies may increase vocabulary size, embedding parameters, and lexical coverage, but vocabulary sizes and parameter-matched controls are absent. There is no Unigram-only baseline, gold morphological-boundary evaluation, or expert annotation. A few selected segmentations and fertility scores—without controlled vocabulary sizes or a specified evaluation corpus—do not demonstrate morphology alignment.

Much of the benchmark performance is at or only slightly above chance. For example, the Bengali base average is 25.22 where the component tasks have approximately 25% chance accuracy, while the purported Hindi transfer results around 31 are close to the approximately 30.6 macro-average chance level. Differences of one or two points are interpreted as model superiority without confidence intervals, significance tests, or replicate runs. Perplexities produced with different language-specific tokenizers are also not directly comparable, so they cannot explain cross-lingual transfer.

Evaluation comparability is insufficiently documented: exact checkpoints, prompts, answer scoring and normalization, harness commit, sample sizes, and baseline reproduction procedures are missing. Base and instruction-tuned systems are mixed, translated-benchmark quality and pretraining contamination are not examined, and macro-averaging tasks with different chance levels obscures absolute capability.

The human evaluation is too weak to repair the automated-evaluation concerns: it uses only ten prompts, ambiguously refers to selecting the “top-3” responses, and reports no prompt set, assignment design, blinding, randomization, uncertainty, or per-dimension results. It also reports Sanskrit agreement despite claiming evaluation only for Bangla and Hindi, and contains an unresolved “Figure ??” reference.

Several numerical and procedural inconsistencies undermine confidence. Telugu results differ between Tables 3/13 and Tables 4/5 (32.22 versus 32.95, including 51.42 versus 54.20 on XStoryCloze); Table 14 gives still other unspecified-checkpoint values. Instruction data are variously described as 23K, 27K, or 15K, and post-editing is described both for all languages and only Hindi/Marathi. Claims of monotonic context gains and outperforming every sub-3B model contradict the reported tables, including Sarvam 2B.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the public collection. The paper omits preprocessing and evaluation code, exact tokenizer training and vocabulary details, random seeds, corpus split/decontamination procedures, packing and sampling choices, and substantive instruction-tuning settings. Sanskrit and mParamanu appear in experiments without adequate data or training descriptions, and the 237M configuration lists a 1024-dimensional hidden state with 18 attention heads, which is incompatible with ordinary equal-sized heads unless an unreported head dimension is used.

The claims of being “fully open-source” and costing under $1,000 require qualification and accounting: the stated CC BY-NC-SA license is non-commercial, corpus redistribution licenses are not established, Google Translate is a proprietary dependency, and it is unclear whether the budget covers one model or the full family, ablations, failed/resumed runs, data processing, and instruction tuning. Overall, the topic and artifacts are interesting, but major soundness and reproducibility revisions—not merely clearer exposition—are required before a Findings recommendation is justified.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant NLP setting: accessible language modeling for five widely spoken, underrepresented, morphologically rich Indian languages. Training compact models on a single GPU could offer genuine practical value.

The intended release includes model weights, language-specific tokenizers, and instruction-tuning data through a public collection. The 5,000 human-authored Bangla instruction-response pairs are potentially useful community resources.

The evaluation spans several languages, model scales, and benchmark families, and the paper attempts factorial ablations of tokenization and data cleaning. It also reports training hours, hyperparameters, inference speed, perplexity, and acknowledged limitations.
The instruction-tuned models show some meaningful gains, particularly for Hindi and Bangla, suggesting that the underlying artifacts may be worth developing despite the current evidential problems.
weaknesses: The central performance claim is overstated. Most pretrained-model results are close to chance: Bangla scores 25.22 on three approximately 25%-chance tasks; Hindi scores 30.97 against an approximately 30.6% average random baseline; and Telugu scores 32.22 against approximately 31.25%. Differences of tenths or a few percentage points are repeatedly called outperformance without confidence intervals, significance tests, multiple seeds, or other uncertainty analysis.

The proposed RoPE method does not establish the claimed hardware efficiency. Compressing position indices does not reduce the quadratic memory or computation of attention and therefore does not itself permit longer sequences to fit. The ablation changes sequence length together with the interpolation factor, apparently also changing tokens processed per step, and lacks the essential standard-RoPE-at-1024 control, matched-token/compute controls, memory measurements, and long-context evaluation. Moreover, the claimed monotonic improvement is contradicted by the Bangla, Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu rows.

The tokenizer evidence is insufficient for claims of morphology alignment. Vocabulary sizes, training samples, score calibration, and the precise SentencePiece decoding procedure are not reported. Adding every Unigram piece enlarges the vocabulary and potentially the parameter count, confounding both fertility and downstream comparisons. Fertility is not a measure of morphological correctness, while the few hand-selected examples provide no gold-boundary evaluation or systematic judgment by linguists.

There are serious internal inconsistencies. Telugu's base average is 32.22 in Tables 3 and 13 but 32.95 in Tables 4 and 5, with XStoryCloze reported as 51.42, 54.20, and 56.06 in different places; the Marathi ARC result is 26.49 or 26.94 depending on the table. The text reports 54.6 GB of data although Table 1 sums to 56.1 GB and includes a 15.8-GB corpus despite claiming all corpora are below 15 GB.

Training and instruction-data accounting is not reproducible. The reported batch sizes, gradient accumulation, sequence lengths, and step counts imply token totals that disagree with Table 3 for Marathi, Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu. The instruction corpus is variously described as 23K examples, 27K examples, or 27K plus 52K Alpaca examples; the main text suggests manual post-editing across translations, whereas the appendix says it was performed only for Hindi and Marathi.

The evaluation protocol omits exact task configurations and sample sizes, prompts/templates, checkpoint revisions, scoring choices, seeds, truncation settings, and baseline adaptation details. It mixes base, instruction-tuned, causal, and encoder-decoder models without demonstrating protocol comparability. Equal-weight averages also combine tasks with different chance levels, obscuring practical performance, and benchmark contamination is not investigated.

The cross-lingual conclusions are unsupported. Per-token perplexities from different languages and tokenizers are not directly comparable, so using Marathi's lower perplexity to explain Hindi transfer is invalid. Near-chance shared-script results do not isolate language transfer from script overlap, and the paper asserts suitability for translation and retrieval without evaluating either task.

The human evaluation uses only ten prompts and lacks the prompts, generation settings, sampling procedure, blinding, rater allocation, uncertainty estimates, and a sufficiently specified rubric. The meaning of evaluating the “top-3 responses” is unclear, the reported kappa values are not reproducible from the description, and an unresolved “Figure ??” reference remains.

The affordability and openness claims need qualification. No pricing calculation supports the under-$1,000 claim, CPU speed lacks hardware and measurement details, and no normalized FLOP or cost comparison is presented. A non-commercial CC BY-NC-SA release is useful open access but is not conventionally open-source, while upstream corpus licenses are not documented.

Overall, the released artifacts may support a valuable revised resource paper, but the current version does not meet Findings-level soundness or reproducibility. Correcting the inconsistent results, rerunning controlled and statistically supported evaluations, and either validating or substantially narrowing the tokenizer and RoPE claims are important revisions that could plausibly be completed for a subsequent cycle.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, clearly ACL-relevant problem: affordable language modeling for five widely spoken but comparatively underserved Indian languages. Releasing compact models, tokenizers, and instruction data could provide substantial community value. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-twd_p5qz/call-51138715e592408cb9e5d2deb12bf93b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The single-GPU, sub-400M design is practically motivated. The paper reports corpus sources, architecture sizes, optimizer settings, training hours, token counts, inference speed, and MFU, offering more engineering detail than many model-release papers.

The evaluation is broad in language and baseline coverage. The instruction-tuned models obtain promising raw zero-shot results for their size, particularly in Bangla, Marathi, and Hindi, suggesting that language-specific compact models merit further study.

The authors attempt tokenizer/data-cleaning ablations, context-length experiments, human evaluation, and documentation of the human-authored Bangla instruction dataset. The limitations section also candidly acknowledges domain limitations, repeated-data training, translation quality, and safety risks.
weaknesses: The central RoPE claim is technically unsupported. Scaling position indices does not reduce the memory or computation of attention over a length-y sequence; the attention and KV tensors still contain y positions. Moreover, the proposed mapping is essentially positional interpolation already cited from Chen et al. (2023). Table 5 changes context length and scaling factor together, lacks an unscaled RoPE control at each context length, and provides no memory or throughput measurements. Longer-context runs also appear to process more tokens, confounding the comparison. Even the claimed monotonic improvement is contradicted by the Bangla, Hindi, and Tamil rows.

The hybrid tokenizer is not specified rigorously enough to validate or reproduce. SentencePiece uses one model type, but the paper says deterministic BPE pieces and Unigram pieces compete through Viterbi search without explaining the resulting model type or how incompatible score scales are calibrated. Vocabulary sizes and parameter-matched controls are absent, so gains may partly reflect a larger union vocabulary. Morphological alignment is supported only by selected examples, some of which are not clearly better; there is no systematic morpheme-boundary evaluation. Fertility is not formally defined, its evaluation corpus is unspecified, and comparisons against tokenizers with different vocabulary sizes do not establish end-to-end cost savings.

The benchmark evidence does not justify the sweeping outperformance claims. Many base-model scores are at or close to random-choice baselines, while numerical wins as small as 0.08 points are treated as meaningful. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-run results. Exact checkpoints, base-versus-instruct variants, prompts/chat templates, answer-scoring and normalization procedures, and LM-Evaluation-Harness revisions are not reported. No benchmark decontamination is performed despite training on web and Wikipedia data.

Numerous internal inconsistencies undermine confidence. The corpus sizes in Table 1 sum to 56.1 GB rather than the stated 54.6 GB; instruction data are variously described as 15K, 23K, and 27K examples, with an additional 52K Hindi Alpaca set introduced only later; Telugu's full-model average is 32.95 in Table 4 but 32.22 in Tables 3 and 13; several zero-shot values in Table 14 conflict with the main tables; and reported steps, batch sizes, gradient accumulation, and sequence lengths do not reproduce several stated token totals.

The ablations do not isolate their claimed causes. BPE versus BPE+Unigram is not matched for vocabulary size or parameter count; cleaned versus uncleaned conditions do not report matched token quantities or data composition; and context length is confounded with scaling, token exposure, and compute. Single runs without uncertainty are especially inadequate for the roughly 0.5–2-point differences being interpreted.

The claimed cross-lingual transfer is not demonstrated: the Sanskrit and Marathi models' Hindi averages are only marginally above a chance-weighted baseline, and no translation or information-retrieval experiment is presented. Perplexities from different languages and tokenizers are not directly comparable, so they cannot substantiate the transfer explanation.

The human evaluation uses only ten prompts and leaves response sampling, the meaning of “top-3,” blinding, rubrics, per-model sample counts, and uncertainty unspecified. The reported Fleiss kappa for the instruction dataset is similarly uninterpretable without the rating labels and number of raters per item. Translation post-editing descriptions conflict, and no credible quality assessment is supplied for Tamil or Telugu.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the linked model collection: there is no code release identified, exact preprocessing rules, tokenizer construction details, random seeds, complete µP configuration, evaluation scripts, or CPU hardware/protocol. Calling a CC BY-NC-SA noncommercial release “open-source” is also misleading. These central validity and reproducibility problems place the paper below Findings, although a substantially corrected and re-evaluated resource paper could reasonably be resubmitted in a future cycle.

strengths: The work addresses a highly relevant problem: affordable language modeling for five widely spoken, morphologically rich Indian languages across four scripts.

Releasing monolingual models, tokenizers, and instruction data is potentially useful to under-resourced research communities. The single-A100 training regime and reported model sizes, hours, token counts, throughput, and MFU are valuable aspects of the intended contribution.
The experimental scope is ambitious, spanning numerous baselines, multiple-choice benchmarks, tokenizer/data-cleaning/context ablations, perplexity, and human evaluation.
Language-specific tokenization and careful corpus cleaning are sensible directions, and the qualitative segmentation examples motivate studying morphology-aware tokenization more rigorously.

The paper is generally well organized and candidly acknowledges limited domain coverage, repeated-data training, translation noise, incomplete convergence, and safety limitations. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-zxt_xohi/call-77b89515e0c64928ba8a3d589d9c4ad3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central competitiveness claim is not adequately supported. Many base-model results are effectively at chance: approximately 25% on four-choice tasks, 33% on XNLI, and 50% on XStoryCloze/XCOPA. Raw accuracies with different chance levels are averaged, while small differences—sometimes only 0.05–0.5 points—are treated as meaningful without sample sizes, confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests.

The proposed RoPE method appears to be standard linear positional interpolation. Scaling position indices does not reduce the attention computation or activation memory required by a longer token sequence, so it cannot by itself accommodate sequences beyond a hardware memory limit. The ablation simultaneously changes context length, interpolation factor, and likely tokens processed; it lacks a same-length standard-RoPE control and any long-context evaluation. Moreover, the reported averages are not monotonic for Bangla, Hindi, or Tamil, contrary to the text.

The hybrid tokenizer is insufficiently specified. A SentencePiece model has one model type, and BPE merge scores and Unigram probabilities are not directly interchangeable; the claimed combination of deterministic BPE merges with Viterbi selection over added Unigram pieces is therefore not reproducible from the description. Vocabulary sizes, score calibration, training settings, and code are absent.

Tokenizer evidence is also confounded: unioning vocabularies can trivially lower fertility, and the ablation does not establish equal vocabulary size, parameter count, raw-text exposure, or compute. A few selected examples and downstream scores near chance do not substantiate the claimed morphological alignment; gold morphological-boundary evaluation is needed.

Numerous internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results. Telugu base averages are 32.22 in Tables 3/13 but 32.95 in Tables 4/5; zero-shot XStoryCloze and XCOPA values in Table 14 disagree with Tables 4 and 10–13. Instruction counts alternate among 23K, 27K, and an additional 52K Hindi Alpaca examples. Reported token totals do not follow from Table 16's batch sizes, accumulation factors, sequence lengths, and stated step counts. The 237M configuration also gives 1,024 dimensions and 18 heads without specifying a compatible head dimension.

Evaluation comparability is unclear because prompt templates, chat formatting, likelihood normalization, model revisions, benchmark versions/splits, example counts, and contamination checks are not reported. Base and instruction-tuned models are mixed, and counting how many larger models are beaten overstates evidence when several baselines themselves score below chance.

The asserted cross-lingual transfer is unsupported. The Sanskrit and multilingual models' Hindi/Marathi averages are essentially chance, and validation perplexities computed on different languages and tokenizers cannot explain cross-language benchmark performance. No translation or retrieval experiment supports the claimed suitability for those tasks.

Instruction-data quality control and human evaluation are under-described. The paper says all translations were post-edited but later says only Hindi and Marathi were; Tamil and Telugu receive no direct quality audit. Fleiss' kappa is unexplained for free-text instruction creation. Human evaluation uses only ten prompts, ambiguously selected “top-3” responses, and reports neither blinding, randomization, per-dimension scores, uncertainty, nor significance.

Although an artifact collection is linked, reproducibility still requires immutable data/model versions, complete preprocessing and evaluation code, random seeds, tokenizer construction code, µP details, instruction-tuning hyperparameters, and a cost calculation supporting the under-$1,000 claim. These validity and reporting problems affect the main technical and empirical claims, so the paper is not presently close to Findings; controlled reruns and substantial correction could plausibly support a next-cycle resubmission.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, clearly ACL-relevant problem: affordable language modeling for five major, morphologically rich Indian languages.
Training and releasing several 108M–367M monolingual models, tokenizers, and instruction datasets is a potentially useful community contribution, especially given the single-GPU constraint.
The evaluation is broad in intended scope, covering multiple languages, model sizes, downstream benchmarks, ablations, perplexity, efficiency, and human judgments.

The 5K human-authored Bengali instruction-response pairs and emphasis on culturally relevant content could constitute a valuable resource if their construction and validation are documented rigorously.
weaknesses: The central competitiveness claim is not convincingly supported. Most pretrained Paramanu results are approximately at chance: 25.22 versus a 25% chance average for Bengali, 30.97 versus about 30.6% for Hindi, 26.40 versus 25% for Marathi, 33.34 versus 31.25% for Tamil, and 32.22 versus 31.25% for Telugu. Many claimed wins are differences of one or two points over other near-chance systems, yet there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated runs.

Reported results are internally inconsistent. Telugu's pretrained average is 32.22 in Tables 3 and 13 but 32.95 in Tables 4 and 5. Table 14's nominal zero-shot XStoryCloze/XCOPA scores disagree with the main task tables. The claimed monotonic context-length improvement is contradicted by results for Bengali, Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu. Instruction-set sizes change between 23K and 27K, and the appendix introduces an additional 52K Hindi Alpaca examples absent from the main methodology.

The RoPE contribution is technically unsupported. The equation is essentially the positional-interpolation method already proposed by Chen et al.; scaling position indices does not reduce the memory needed to process the longer token sequence and therefore cannot make an otherwise hardware-infeasible context fit. The ablation changes interpolation factor and sequence length simultaneously, lacks an ordinary-RoPE control at the same length, evaluates no long-context task, and never exceeds the reported 1,024-token model context.

The tokenizer method is not specified as a reproducible algorithm: a SentencePiece model has a particular model type, while the paper simultaneously describes deterministic BPE merges and Unigram Viterbi scoring. Vocabulary sizes are omitted, and augmenting BPE with all Unigram pieces confounds morphology with vocabulary size, parameter count, and fertility. The evidence for morphological alignment consists mainly of selected examples—some unchanged or more fragmented—without gold morphological segmentation evaluation. Small single-run benchmark differences cannot isolate the tokenizer's effect.

Evaluation details needed for a fair comparison are missing, including exact checkpoint revisions, task versions and sample counts, prompts/templates, answer scoring and normalization, decoding settings, seeds, and uncertainty. Base and instruction-tuned systems are mixed, heterogeneous task accuracies with different chance levels are macro-averaged, and no contamination analysis is performed despite web pretraining data and translated instruction data.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper omits vocabulary sizes, corpus versions, preprocessing thresholds, sampling/packing details, initialization and seeds, and executable training/evaluation code. Reported corpus totals and training token counts conflict with the batch sizes, gradient accumulation, sequence lengths, and step counts; for example, the stated Hindi configuration implies about 78.6B tokens rather than 66B. The sub-$1,000 claim provides no hardware price or accounting basis.

Instruction-data quality control is unclear and contradictory: the main text suggests manual post-editing for all translated languages, whereas the appendix says only Hindi and Marathi were post-edited. Fleiss' kappa is reported without defining the categorical judgments or shared annotation items, and the stated word-error rates have no reference construction. Annotator recruitment, compensation, consent, and dataset splits are also absent.

The human evaluation uses only ten prompts and ambiguously refers to selecting the 'top-3 responses'; it provides no prompt set, sampling protocol, blinding, per-dimension results, uncertainty, or statistical analysis. It unexpectedly reports Sanskrit agreement despite describing only Bengali and Hindi evaluation and refers to a missing figure.

Conclusions substantially exceed the evidence. Near-chance shared-script results do not establish suitability for translation or information retrieval, and experiments on one model family without a compute- and data-matched multilingual control cannot establish that monolingual training is the optimal strategy. Substantial controlled rerunning, reconciliation of the results, and reframing of the methodological claims are required before the work meets Findings-level soundness and reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important CL problem: affordable language modeling for five widely spoken, morphologically rich Indian languages under realistic single-GPU constraints.

Provides a potentially useful collection of compact models, tokenizers, and instruction-tuning data, with named corpus sources and partial reporting of architectures, training hours, token counts, and efficiency.
The empirical scope is broad, covering multiple languages, tasks, model sizes, ablations, baselines, perplexity, inference speed, and an attempted human evaluation.
The instruction-tuned Hindi and Bangla results provide a promising signal that compact language-specific models can be practically useful.
weaknesses: The headline competitiveness claim is not adequately supported. Most pretrained-model results are approximately at random-chance levels: about 25% for MMLU, ARC, Belebele, and HellaSwag; 50% for XStoryCloze and XCOPA; and 33% for XNLI. Many claimed wins are only 1–2 points, but no sample sizes, confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported.

The comparisons mix base and instruction-tuned systems and average raw accuracies across tasks with different chance levels. Hindi additionally uses 52K synthetic Alpaca examples, making several comparisons unequal. Prompt templates, scoring details, model revisions, and contamination checks are absent.

The claimed RoPE contribution appears to be the existing positional-interpolation method of Chen et al. (2023), rather than a new method. Scaling position indices does not reduce the attention memory required by a longer token sequence, and the paper incorrectly says relative distances are preserved when they are divided by alpha. There is no same-length standard-RoPE baseline, long-context evaluation, or memory/throughput evidence. Table 5 also confounds scaling factor with context length and likely training-token count; its stated monotonic trend is contradicted by several rows.

The hybrid tokenizer is insufficiently and possibly inconsistently specified: a SentencePiece model has one model type, yet the paper simultaneously claims deterministic BPE operation and Unigram-style Viterbi decoding. Vocabulary sizes, score calibration, and parameter-matched controls are missing. Adding an entire Unigram vocabulary trivially increases capacity and can lower fertility, while morphological alignment is supported only by selected examples rather than gold morphological-boundary evaluation.

The ablations are single-run, near-chance comparisons without uncertainty or controls for vocabulary size, data amount, and tokens processed. Some numbers are inconsistent: Telugu's full-model average is 32.22 in the main results but 32.95 in the ablation, and the claimed Hindi tokenizer gain of 1.41 points does not match the displayed 30.97 versus 29.87 scores.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings. Missing details include exact vocabulary construction, corpus versions and preprocessing rules, MuP configuration, instruction-tuning hyperparameters, seeds, evaluation configurations, software/code versions, and model/data hashes. Reported training-token totals are difficult to reconcile with the stated batch sizes, gradient accumulation, sequence lengths, and step counts. Sanskrit and mParamanu experiments are introduced without corresponding training-data documentation.

Dataset and human-evaluation reporting contains contradictions: the main text says translations into all four languages were manually post-edited, whereas the appendix says only Hindi and Marathi were; instruction totals vary between 23K and 27K. The human study uses only ten prompts, leaves “top-3 responses” undefined, provides no blinding, assignment protocol, uncertainty, or dimension-level results, and reports kappa values without enough information to establish their validity.

Claims of effective cross-lingual transfer and suitability for translation or information retrieval are speculative because those tasks are not evaluated. Comparing perplexities across models with different tokenizers is not meaningful evidence of transfer.

The non-commercial CC BY-NC-SA release should not be described unqualifiedly as “open source,” and corpus licensing, annotator compensation/consent, translated-data quality, and safety analysis need fuller documentation. Overall, substantial experimental and reporting revisions are required before the work meets the soundness and reproducibility bar for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important ACL-relevant problem and provides a practically motivated collection of compact models, tokenizers, and instruction data for five underrepresented Indian languages.

Training sub-400M models on a single A100 is a useful accessibility contribution. The manuscript reports architecture configurations, token counts, training hours, corpus sources, and several acknowledged limitations.

The evaluation is broad in coverage, spanning multiple languages, benchmarks, model sizes, ablations, and human assessment. Instruction tuning produces notable improvements for Bangla and especially Hindi.
The language-specific tokenization direction and the creation of 5,000 human-authored Bangla instruction-response pairs are promising resource contributions.
weaknesses: The central performance claims are not adequately supported. Many reported scores are at or only slightly above task chance levels—for example, the claimed Hindi transfer from Marathi/Sanskrit is approximately random performance. Numerous model differences are fractions of a percentage point, yet there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated runs. Consequently, rankings such as “outperforms” and “strong cross-lingual transfer” are unreliable.

The proposed RoPE method is essentially positional interpolation, and scaling position indices does not reduce the attention or activation memory required to process a longer sequence. Its ablation simultaneously increases context length from 256 to 1024 and, under the fixed-step setup, increases training tokens fourfold. Without an unscaled RoPE baseline at the same sequence length, equal-token/compute controls, and memory measurements, neither the performance attribution nor the claimed hardware efficiency is valid.

The hybrid tokenizer is insufficiently specified and appears internally inconsistent: a SentencePiece BPE model does not perform the stated Unigram-style Viterbi decoding merely by appending Unigram pieces. Vocabulary sizes, model type, score reconciliation, and parameter-count controls are missing. Lower fertility may simply follow from a larger vocabulary, while morphological alignment is supported only by selected examples rather than a gold segmentation benchmark or expert evaluation.

The comparison mixes base and instruction-tuned systems and emphasizes raw averages across tasks with different chance levels. Several conclusions overstate the tables: the claim of outperforming all models below 3B has explicit Sarvam-2B exceptions, and efficiency is inferred from incomparable parameter/token/hour figures without controlled baseline latency, cost, or hardware measurements.

Reproducibility is below Findings standard. The paper links a Hugging Face collection but provides no training/evaluation code, exact model revisions, seeds, prompt or chat templates, tokenizer sizes, detailed filtering rules, data-ordering/epoch information, or benchmark sample counts. There is also no train/test contamination analysis despite repeated training over web corpora. Reported corpus totals are inconsistent (54.6 GB versus 56.1 GB in Table 1, and “less than 15 GB” despite Hindi being 15.8 GB).

The human and dataset evaluations are too under-specified to repair the automated evidence. Human evaluation uses only ten prompts, provides no uncertainty, and leaves “top-3 responses” unexplained. Annotator overlap, compensation, rating protocol, and the computation of Fleiss' kappa are unclear; Bengali/Hindi/Sanskrit descriptions conflict, and an unresolved “Figure ??” remains. Claims about translation post-editing and word-error rates are likewise inconsistent.

The paper incorrectly uses token-level perplexities from different languages/tokenizers to explain cross-lingual transfer and extrapolates chance-level results to translation and information retrieval without evaluating those tasks. These validity issues require new controlled experiments and substantial claim revision before the work is suitable for Findings.

Lower fertility and a few selected examples do not demonstrate morphological alignment; no gold-boundary evaluation or systematic linguistic judgment is provided, and the ablation may confound vocabulary or parameter count.

Most base-model benchmark results are approximately at random-choice performance. Small differences—often below one or two points—are repeatedly described as models “outperforming” competitors without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Raw accuracies from tasks with different chance baselines are averaged, further weakening interpretation. Dataset sizes, prompts, checkpoint identifiers, harness versions, and scoring details are also missing.

The broad conclusion that monolingual models are the optimal constrained strategy is not supported by controlled evidence. Baselines vary greatly in data, instruction tuning, tokenizer, context length, and training objectives, and there is no compute-, data-, vocabulary-, and parameter-matched multilingual baseline. The reported mParamanu comparison is not an adequate control because its training languages and configuration differ.

There are pervasive internal inconsistencies. The listed corpus sizes sum to 56.1 GB rather than the stated 54.6 GB; instruction data are variously described as 23K and 27K; post-editing is claimed for all translated languages in the main text but only Hindi and Marathi in the appendix; nominally identical Telugu and other results differ across Tables 4, 5, and 13; and most reported token totals do not agree with batch size × gradient accumulation × sequence length × training steps. The 237M configuration also gives a 1024-dimensional state with 18 standard attention heads, which is not divisible, while Sanskrit and several mParamanu variants receive little methodological description.

Reproducibility falls substantially below the Findings bar. The manuscript does not identify training/evaluation code, immutable artifact versions, exact data splits and cleaning rules, unique-token and epoch counts, tokenizer configurations, µP parameterization, instruction-tuning hyperparameters, or complete training logs. Dataset provenance and licensing are underdeveloped, and calling a CC BY-NC-SA release “open-source” overstates the accessibility of a noncommercial artifact.

The human evaluation is too weakly documented to support the qualitative claims: only ten prompts are used, “top-3 responses” suggests an unexplained selection step, and prompts, sampling settings, rater assignments, aggregation, uncertainty, and compensation are omitted. Reported Sanskrit agreement is inconsistent with the stated Bangla/Hindi evaluation, and a promised agreement figure remains an unresolved “Figure ??” reference.

The resource premise is worthwhile, but reaching soundness would require correcting or removing the RoPE claim, precisely implementing and validating the tokenizer, running matched and statistically rigorous evaluations, reconciling the results, and supplying reproducible artifacts. This is substantial reconstruction unlikely to fit the next review cycle.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-blor8915/call-17958765cd164f89b445a8923e1072a3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important CL need by developing compact models and instruction data for five under-served Indian languages; releasing the models and tokenizers increases the potential resource value.
The empirical scope is broad, covering multiple languages, model scales, benchmark families, and ablations of tokenization, cleaning, and context length.

The paper reports corpus sources, architecture configurations, optimization settings, GPU hours, throughput, and several genuine limitations, including repeated-data training, narrow domains, machine-translation artifacts, and absent safety mechanisms.
Single-GPU training of 108M–367M-parameter models is practically relevant, and some instruction-tuned results—notably Hindi—justify further investigation.
weaknesses: The central performance claim is not convincingly supported. Base-model averages are approximately chance: 25.22 for Bangla versus roughly 25% chance, 30.97 for Hindi versus roughly 30.6% after averaging its heterogeneous tasks, and 33.34/32.22 for Tamil/Telugu versus roughly 31.25%. Many claimed wins are only fractions of a point, with no seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or sample counts. Averaging raw accuracies across tasks with different chance levels further obscures capability.

The purported RoPE method is essentially the positional interpolation of Chen et al. Rescaling position indices cannot reduce the attention-memory cost of processing more tokens, contrary to the hardware-efficiency motivation. Its ablation changes alpha and physical context length simultaneously, lacks an unscaled same-length control and long-context evaluation, and therefore cannot isolate any interpolation benefit. The stated monotonic trend is also contradicted by several table entries.

The tokenizer contribution is insufficiently defined and controlled. The account of deterministic BPE pieces competing through Viterbi decoding is technically unclear; vocabulary sizes, scores, training settings, and exact algorithm are omitted. Augmenting the vocabulary may change parameter count and capacity, yet there is no size-matched BPE control, Unigram-only baseline, or gold morphological evaluation. A few selected segmentations and unmatched fertility comparisons do not establish morphology alignment.

The broad conclusions about efficiency, cross-lingual transfer, and monolingual optimality exceed the evidence. There are no compute-matched monolingual/multilingual baselines or comparative latency measurements, while Sanskrit-to-Hindi and Marathi-to-Hindi scores are essentially at chance. Translation and retrieval suitability are asserted without evaluating either task.

Numerous inconsistencies undermine reliability: the listed corpora sum to 56.1 GB rather than the stated 54.6 GB; Hindi violates the claimed under-15-GB limit; instruction data are variously reported as 23K or 27K, with an additional 52K Hindi Alpaca set introduced only later; manual post-editing is described both for all translated languages and only Hindi/Marathi; and nominally identical model results differ across tables, such as Telugu 32.22 versus 32.95. The reported Hindi tokenizer gain is 1.10 points from the table, not 1.41.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the artifact release: there is no training/evaluation code link, exact data snapshots, vocabulary specifications, tokenizer implementation, random seeds, packing or checkpoint-selection procedure, evaluation prompts and harness version, contamination analysis, or instruction-tuning hyperparameters. Corpus licensing is also insufficiently audited, and calling a CC BY-NC-SA release “open source” is misleading.

The human evaluation cannot substantiate generation quality: it uses only ten prompts and ambiguously selected “top-3 responses,” without decoding settings, blinding, randomization, uncertainty, or criterion-level results. Agreement is reported for Sanskrit despite the stated evaluation covering only Bangla and Hindi, and a referenced agreement figure is missing. Overall, substantial experimental and reporting revisions are needed before the work meets Findings-level soundness and reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important ACL-relevant gap by developing compact generative models for five widely spoken but underrepresented Indian languages under realistic compute constraints.
Releases a substantial collection of models, language-specific tokenizers, and instruction-tuning data; these artifacts could be useful foundations for regional NLP research.
Includes broad baseline comparisons and attempts to isolate tokenization, data cleaning, context length, instruction tuning, cross-script transfer, inference efficiency, and human judgments.
The paper is generally organized clearly and candidly acknowledges limited domain coverage, repeated-data training, incomplete convergence, translation noise, and safety limitations.
weaknesses: The headline competitiveness claim is not adequately supported. Most pretrained-model results are at or only slightly above task-specific chance levels—for example, approximately 25 on four-choice tasks and 50 on two-choice tasks—yet small differences are interpreted as meaningful wins. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, multiple training seeds, evaluation-set sizes, or variance estimates.

The proposed RoPE technique appears to be standard linear positional interpolation already described by Chen et al. Scaling position IDs does not itself reduce the memory required to process a longer sequence, and the paper incorrectly says relative offsets are preserved even though they are divided by alpha. The ablation does not establish a fixed token/compute budget and includes no long-context evaluation, leaving both the novelty and claimed efficiency benefit unsupported.

The tokenizer contribution is insufficiently specified and validated: vocabulary sizes, tokenizer-training settings, score calibration when combining BPE and Unigram vocabularies, fertility definition, and fertility evaluation corpus are absent. Morphological alignment is inferred from a few selected examples rather than evaluated against morphological boundaries, while fertility comparisons may be confounded by vocabulary size.

Several inconsistencies materially undermine reproducibility: the instruction corpus is variously reported as 23K and 27K examples; an additional 52K-example Hindi Alpaca corpus appears only in the appendix; the main text suggests post-editing for all translated languages whereas the appendix says only Hindi and Marathi were post-edited; and Telugu and n-shot zero-shot scores differ across tables without explanation. Reported steps, batch configurations, and token totals are also difficult to reconcile.

The cross-lingual-transfer conclusion is overstated. Sanskrit and multilingual models obtain averages around the aggregate random baseline on Hindi and Marathi tasks, so scores such as 31.05 on Hindi and 25.26 on Marathi do not demonstrate strong transfer. Perplexities measured on different languages and language-specific tokenizers are not directly comparable and cannot explain transfer performance.

Evaluation is dominated by translated multiple-choice benchmarks and simple unnormalized task averages. The human evaluation covers only ten prompts and omits essential details about response selection, decoding, blinding, assignment, and uncertainty. The reported Fleiss kappa for independently authored instruction-response pairs is also unexplained.

The linked model collection does not substitute for a documented reproducible pipeline: code, exact model/tokenizer configurations, evaluation prompts and harness settings, dataset versions, random seeds, decontamination checks, CPU hardware, and a cost calculation supporting the under-$1,000 claim are not provided. These issues require substantial revision before the work meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.
